description: At 1.8 million words, the Mahabharata is the longest poem in the world. A war between cousins, a god as charioteer, and a lesson about duty.

hero.hook: Ten times Homer, a war between cousins, and a god at the reins of a chariot.

blocks.text: The **Mahabharata** is not a novel. It is the longest epic poem ever composed: about **1.8 million words**, ten times the Iliad and the Odyssey put together. Its Sanskrit title means “the great story of the Bharatas,” a royal line of ancient India.

At the center: a war between brothers for the throne of [[Hastinapura]], the mythical capital of the north. Two branches of the same family tear each other apart. In the middle of the chaos, one sacred dialogue changes everything: the [[Bhagavad-Gita]], one of the most read texts in Hinduism.

The Mahabharata is credited to the sage **Vyasa**, who is both its author and a character in it. In fact the text took shape over nearly eight centuries, between **400 BC** and **AD 400**, out of a long oral tradition.

blocks.caption: Vyasa, the legendary sage credited with the Mahabharata

blocks.text: Legend says Vyasa dictated so fast that the god **Ganesha** broke off one of his tusks to use as a pen and lose nothing.

The work has **18 parvas** (books) and about **100,000** couplets. It is not only a war story: it is a [[Somme]] of Indian knowledge, taking in politics, morality, cosmology and nested myths. A saying goes: “What is not in the Mahabharata is nowhere.” It also shows the shift from the old Vedic religion to classical [[Brahmanism]].

sections.title: How an encyclopedia of the soul came together

blocks.text: On one side, the five **Pandava** brothers, sons of King Pandu and models of virtue. On the other, the hundred **Kaurava**, sons of the blind king **Dhritarashtra** and led by the ambitious **Duryodhana**. A rigged game of dice ruins the Pandava: they lose their kingdom and go into exile for thirteen years.

blocks.caption: The battle of Kurukshetra, the warlike heart of the Mahabharata

blocks.text: When they come back, **Krishna**, prince of the Yadava and ally of the Pandava, tries to mediate. The Kaurava refuse. War breaks out on the plain of **Kurukshetra** and lasts **18 days**. Teachers against students, cousins against cousins: [[Dharma]], moral duty, collides with the claims of blood. The Pandava win, but the warrior caste is almost wiped out.

sections.title: The machinery of the war of Kurukshetra

blocks.text: Just before the first clash, the archer **Arjuna**, the most feared of the Pandava, sees his uncles, his friends and his teachers in the enemy ranks. He drops his bow. His charioteer, **Krishna** (an avatar of the god Vishnu), answers him in the **Bhagavad-Gita**: about **700** verses on duty and action.

blocks.caption: Krishna guides Arjuna on the chariot, on the edge of battle

blocks.text: In 1945, the physicist **Robert Oppenheimer**, who had learned Sanskrit, quoted Krishna after the first atomic test: “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.”

Krishna teaches **Karma Yoga**: act according to your duty, without clinging to the fruits of the action. Kurukshetra then becomes the mirror of an inner struggle. The battlefield is also talking about conscience.

sections.title: The sacred dialogue of the Bhagavad-Gita

blocks.text: The Mahabharata shaped the ethics of Southeast Asia. In the 20th century, **Gandhi** read the Bhagavad-Gita as a “dictionary of conduct,” turning the war into an allegory of the struggle within. The theater of **Peter Brook** and huge Indian television series carried the epic to hundreds of millions of viewers.
Why does the text last? Because it refuses easy answers. It puts everyone in front of impossible choices, and turns the battlefield into a mirror of conscience.

The **Mahabharata**, the longest poem in the world, tells the war of **Kurukshetra** between the Pandava and the Kaurava, and holds the **Bhagavad-Gita**, where Krishna teaches selfless action and **Dharma**.
